dy/dt + p y = q.title: First-order linear ODE in standard form
dy/dt + p y = q.about: Any first-order equation that is linear in y and y′ can be put in this form by dividing through by the coefficient of dy/dt. It models RC and RL circuits, Newton cooling, mixing tanks and first-order sensor lag, and it is always solvable with an integrating factor.
assumptions: y and dy/dt appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together; a y^{2} or sin(y) term makes it nonlinear
p(t) and q(t) are continuous on the interval of interest; the solution exists and is unique there for any initial value
Divide by the leading coefficient first: 3y′ + 6y = 12 becomes y′ + 2y = 4
q = 0 is the homogeneous case, which is also separable
vars: coefficient of y; 1/p is the time constant when p is constant
related: constant p and q: final value plus decaying transient
time constant; 63.2% of the way to the final value after one τ

example.problem: Solve dy/dt + 2y = 4 with y(0) = 0 and find y at t = 1.
steps: p = 2 and q = 4 are constant, so the final value is q/p = 2

μ = e^{∫ p dt}.title: Integrating factor for a linear first-order ODE
μ = e^{∫ p dt}.about: Multiplying y′ + p y = q by μ turns the left side into the derivative of a product, (μy)′ = μq, which can then be integrated directly. Any antiderivative of p works; the constant of integration can be dropped.
assumptions: The equation must be in standard form y′ + p y = q, with a leading coefficient of 1
p(t) must be integrable on the interval; μ is then positive and never zero
Drop the constant in ∫ p dt; it only scales μ and cancels out
Watch signs: for y′ − 3y = q, p = −3 and μ = e^{−3t}
vars: coefficient of y in standard form
related: why it works: μ′ = p μ
when p = k/t, since e^{k ln t} = t^{k}

example.problem: Find the integrating factor for y′ + 2t y = t and evaluate it at t = 1.
steps: p = 2t, so ∫ p dt = t^{2} (constant dropped)

y = (1/μ)(∫ μ q dt + C).title: General solution of a linear first-order ODE
y = (1/μ)(∫ μ q dt + C).about: After multiplying by the integrating factor, integrate both sides of (μy)′ = μq and divide by μ. The C term is the homogeneous (transient) part; the rest is a particular solution. One initial condition fixes C.
assumptions: Valid wherever p and q are continuous; the solution can blow up only where they do
Include C before dividing by μ; adding it afterwards is a common mistake
If ∫ μ q dt has no closed form, leave it as a definite integral from t_{0} to t
vars: constant fixed by the initial condition
related: same thing with the initial value built in

example.problem: Solve y′ + y = t with y(0) = 1 and find y(1).

∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(t) dt.title: Separation of variables for dy/dt = f(t) g(y)
∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(t) dt.about: When the right side factors into a function of t times a function of y, move every y to one side and every t to the other and integrate both. It covers growth and decay, logistic growth, draining tanks (Torricelli) and many rate laws.
assumptions: The right side must factor as f(t)·g(y); t + y does not separate
Dividing by g(y) loses any constant solution where g(y) = 0; check those separately
Only one constant of integration is needed, on one side
The result is often implicit; solve for y when possible and pick the sign that fits the initial value

example.problem: Solve dy/dt = t/y with y(0) = 2 and find y(1.5).

y = y_{0} e^{kt}.title: Exponential growth and decay
y = y_{0} e^{kt}.about: The solution of dy/dt = k y: the rate of change is proportional to the amount present. k > 0 grows (bacteria, compound interest), k < 0 decays (radioactivity, RC discharge, a cooling temperature difference).
assumptions: The rate constant k stays fixed over the whole time span
Nothing else adds or removes y; with a constant source use y′ = k y + q instead
Real growth saturates eventually; for large t a logistic model is usually better
related: time constant; e^{−1} = 36.8% left after one τ

example.problem: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. How much of a 100 g sample remains after 2000 years?

a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0.title: Homogeneous second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients
a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0.about: The model for unforced mass-spring-damper systems (m x′′ + c x′ + k x = 0) and series RLC circuits. Trying y = e^{rt} reduces it to the characteristic equation, and the kind of roots decides whether the response is overdamped, critically damped or oscillating.
assumptions: a, b, c are constants, with a ≠ 0; variable coefficients need other methods
Homogeneous: no forcing term. With forcing, add a particular solution to this one
Linear: in a real system this holds for small motions (small angles, linear springs and dampers)

example.problem: A 2 kg mass on a 50 N/m spring has damping 8 N·s/m. Find ζ and the damped frequency.

a r^{2} + b r + c = 0.title: Characteristic equation of a constant-coefficient ODE
a r^{2} + b r + c = 0.about: Substituting y = e^{rt} into a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0 and dividing out e^{rt} leaves this quadratic. Its two roots set the form of the solution and the system's behaviour.
assumptions: Only for linear ODEs with constant coefficients
The discriminant b^{2} − 4ac decides the case: > 0 real distinct, = 0 repeated, < 0 complex pair
For stability (decay to zero) both roots need negative real parts; with a > 0 that means b > 0 and c > 0
related: in terms of damping ratio and natural frequency
an nth-order ODE gives an nth-degree polynomial

example.problem: Find the characteristic roots of y′′ + 5y′ + 6y = 0.
steps: Both negative: the response decays without oscillating (overdamped)

Real and distinct ‖ y = c_{1} e^{r_{1}t}.title: Solution for real, distinct characteristic roots
Real and distinct ‖ y = c_{1} e^{r_{1}t}.about: When b^{2} − 4ac > 0 the solution is a sum of two exponentials. With both roots negative the system is overdamped: it returns to rest without overshooting, more slowly than with critical damping.
assumptions: r_{1} ≠ r_{2}, both real (b^{2} > 4ac)
Two initial conditions, y(0) and y′(0), fix c_{1} and c_{2}
Long-term behaviour is set by the root closest to zero (the slowest mode)

example.problem: Solve y′′ + 5y′ + 6y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0 and find y(1).

Repeated ‖ y = (c_{1} + c_{2} t) e^{rt}.title: Solution for a repeated characteristic root
Repeated ‖ y = (c_{1} + c_{2} t) e^{rt}.about: When b^{2} = 4ac there is only one root r = −b/(2a), and the second independent solution is t e^{rt}. For a damped system this is critical damping: the fastest return to rest without overshoot.
assumptions: Exactly b^{2} − 4ac = 0; in practice this is a design target and real systems are slightly over or under
The t e^{rt} term can make the response rise briefly before decaying, but it crosses zero at most once

example.problem: Solve y′′ + 4y′ + 4y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0 and find y(1).

Complex, α ± jβ ‖ y = e^{αt} (c_{1} cos(.title: Solution for complex characteristic roots
Complex, α ± jβ ‖ y = e^{αt} (c_{1} cos(.about: When b^{2} < 4ac the roots are α ± jβ and the response oscillates at β rad/s inside an exponential envelope e^{αt}. This is the underdamped case: a ringing spring, an RLC circuit, a pendulum with friction.
assumptions: α < 0 decays, α = 0 oscillates forever (no damping), α > 0 grows (unstable)
Use radians in cos and sin

example.problem: Solve y′′ + 2y′ + 5y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0 and find y(1).

W = y_{1} y′_{2} − y_{2} y′_{1}.title: Wronskian: test for independent solutions
W = y_{1} y′_{2} − y_{2} y′_{1}.about: The Wronskian checks whether two solutions of a second-order linear ODE are independent, so that c_{1}y_{1} + c_{2}y_{2} is the general solution. It is also the denominator in variation of parameters.
assumptions: For solutions of the same linear ODE, W is either zero everywhere or never zero (Abel's theorem)
W ≠ 0 at one point means independent; for arbitrary functions W = 0 does not by itself prove dependence
For n solutions it is the determinant of the n × n matrix of the functions and their derivatives
related: variation of parameters, y′′ + p y′ + q y = g

example.problem: Show that y_{1} = e^{−2t} and y_{2} = e^{−3t} are independent solutions of y′′ + 5y′ + 6y = 0.
steps: e^{−5t} is never zero, so W ≠ 0 everywhere

x′ = A x.title: Linear system of first-order ODEs
x′ = A x.about: Any nth-order linear ODE, and any set of coupled linear ODEs, can be written as one vector equation x′ = A x. This is the state-space form used in controls and vibration; the eigenvalues of A decide stability and the natural modes.
assumptions: A is a constant n × n matrix; linearize a nonlinear system about an equilibrium first
Stable (all solutions decay) when every eigenvalue of A has a negative real part
With an input, x′ = A x + B u, add a particular solution
related: modal solution, A v = λ v
turning y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0 into a system

example.problem: Write y′′ + 5y′ + 6y = 0 as a first-order system and find the eigenvalues of A.
steps: λ = −2, −3: both negative, so the system is stable

x = v e^{λt}.title: Modal solution of x′ = A x
x = v e^{λt}.about: Each eigenpair (λ, v) of A gives a solution that keeps the shape v and grows or decays as e^{λt}. With n independent eigenvectors the general solution is the sum c_{1}v_{1}e^{λ_{1}t} + … + c_{n}v_{n}e^{λ_{n}t}, with the c's set by x(0).
assumptions: A must have n independent eigenvectors (true when the eigenvalues are distinct); otherwise generalized eigenvectors are needed
Complex λ = α ± jβ gives oscillating real solutions e^{αt}(cos, sin) combinations
The eigenvector's scale is arbitrary; the constants c_{i} absorb it
related: solve for the constants, V = [v_{1} … v_{n}]

example.problem: Solve x′ = [1 2; 2 1] x with x(0) = (2, 0) and find x_{1} at t = 0.5.

∂u/∂t = α ∂^{2}u/∂x^{2}.title: Heat (diffusion) equation
∂u/∂t = α ∂^{2}u/∂x^{2}.about: Temperature in a rod changes at a rate proportional to its curvature in x: hot spots flatten out over time. The same equation describes diffusion of a chemical and other smoothing processes. Separation of variables gives sine modes that decay exponentially, the short wavelengths fastest.
assumptions: One-dimensional conduction: the rod is insulated along its sides, heat flows only along x
Constant properties: α = k/(ρ c_{p}) does not change with temperature
No internal heat generation (add a source term otherwise)
Needs an initial temperature profile and a condition at each end
related: u = Σ b_{n} sin(nπx/L) e^{−α(nπ/L)^{2} t}
solution with both ends held at 0
Fourier coefficients of the initial profile f(x)

example.problem: An aluminium rod 0.5 m long (α = 9.7 × 10^{−5} m^{2}/s) starts with temperature sin(πx/L) above ambient, ends held at ambient. What fraction of the peak remains after 60 s?
steps: The first mode decays as e^{−α(π/L)^{2} t}

∂^{2}u/∂t^{2} = c^{2} ∂^{2}u/∂x^{2}.title: Wave equation
∂^{2}u/∂t^{2} = c^{2} ∂^{2}u/∂x^{2}.about: Describes small vibrations of strings, sound in pipes, waves on a beam's axis and electrical signals on lossless lines. Disturbances travel at speed c in both directions without changing shape (d'Alembert).
assumptions: Small displacements, so slopes are small and the equation stays linear
Uniform medium: constant tension and mass per length (string), so c is constant
No damping and no stiffness effects; real strings and beams lose energy and disperse
Needs initial displacement and velocity, plus a condition at each end
related: string, tension T and mass per length μ
natural frequencies of a string fixed at both ends

example.problem: A 0.65 m guitar string has tension 70 N and mass 0.4 g/m. Find its fundamental frequency.

∂^{2}u/∂x^{2} + ∂^{2}u/∂y^{2} = 0.title: Laplace equation
∂^{2}u/∂x^{2} + ∂^{2}u/∂y^{2} = 0.about: The steady-state form of the heat equation in 2-D: temperature with no more change in time. It also governs electrostatic potential in charge-free space, ideal (potential) flow and seepage. A solution has no local maximum or minimum inside the region; each value is the average of its neighbours.
assumptions: Steady state: no time dependence, no sources inside the region (with sources it becomes Poisson's equation)
Homogeneous, isotropic medium
Fully determined by the values (or fluxes) on the boundary
related: short form, any number of dimensions
rectangle a × b, top edge u = f(x), other edges 0
finite-difference form: each node is the mean of its neighbours

example.problem: A 1 × 1 square plate has its top edge held at u = sin(πx) and the other three edges at 0. Find u at the centre.

x_{n+1} = x_{n} − f(x_{n})/f′(x_{n}).title: Newton's method for roots
x_{n+1} = x_{n} − f(x_{n})/f′(x_{n}).about: Follow the tangent line at x_{n} down to where it crosses zero, and repeat. Near a simple root the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step (quadratic convergence), so a few iterations usually suffice.
assumptions: Needs the derivative f′ and a starting guess reasonably close to the root
Fails or jumps away where f′(x_{n}) ≈ 0 (flat spots, local extrema)
At a repeated root convergence slows to linear
Can cycle or diverge from a bad start; bracket with bisection first if unsure

example.problem: Use Newton's method on f(x) = x^{2} − 2 from x_{0} = 1 to estimate √2.

x_{n+1} = x_{n} − f(x_{n})(x_{n} − x_{n−.title: Secant method for roots
x_{n+1} = x_{n} − f(x_{n})(x_{n} − x_{n−.about: Newton's method with the derivative replaced by the slope through the last two points. It needs no derivative and only one new function value per step, and converges superlinearly (order ≈ 1.618).
assumptions: Needs two starting points; they don't have to bracket the root
Fails when f(x_{n}) = f(x_{n−1}) (division by zero) and can diverge from poor starts
Unlike bisection and false position, it does not keep the root bracketed
related: same formula, but keeps one point on each side of the root

example.problem: Apply the secant method to f(x) = x^{2} − 2 with x_{0} = 1, x_{1} = 2. Find x_{3}.

|e_{n}| ≤ (b − a)/2^{n}.title: Bisection method error bound
|e_{n}| ≤ (b − a)/2^{n}.about: Bisection halves a bracketing interval [a, b] each step, keeping the half where f changes sign. It is slow (one binary digit per step) but it always converges, and this bound tells you in advance how many steps you need.
assumptions: f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs
Finds one root in the bracket; with several roots inside, which one is not controlled
Can't find roots where f touches zero without crossing (even multiplicity)
Here the estimate is the midpoint of the interval after n halvings; some texts bound by (b − a)/2^{n+1}

example.problem: How many bisection steps on [1, 2] guarantee the root of x^{2} − 2 to within 10^{−6}?

f′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − f(x))/h.title: Forward difference for the first derivative
f′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − f(x))/h.about: The slope of the secant line from x to x + h. It is the simplest derivative estimate, used at the start of a data set and in explicit time stepping, but its error is first order in h.
assumptions: f is smooth (twice differentiable) near x
Truncation error ≈ (h/2) f′′(x): halving h only halves the error
h can't be too small: rounding error grows like ε/h, so h ≈ √ε ≈ 10^{−8} is the practical floor in double precision
With measured data, noise is amplified by 1/h

example.problem: Estimate the derivative of e^{x} at x = 0 with h = 0.1.
steps: Exact value 1: error 0.0517 ≈ h/2 × f′′ = 0.05, as predicted

f′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − f(x − h))/(2h).title: Central difference for the first derivative
f′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − f(x − h))/(2h).about: The slope between points on either side of x. The leading error terms cancel by symmetry, so it is second-order accurate: halving h cuts the error by four. It is the default choice for interior points.
assumptions: f is smooth (three times differentiable) near x
Truncation error ≈ (h^{2}/6) f′′′(x)
Needs data on both sides, so it can't be used at the ends of a data set
Rounding error still grows as h shrinks; h ≈ 10^{−5} is a good choice in double precision

example.problem: Estimate the derivative of e^{x} at x = 0 with h = 0.1.
steps: Error 0.00167 ≈ h^{2}/6 = 0.00167, 30 times smaller than the forward difference

f′′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − 2f(x) + f(x − h))/h.title: Central difference for the second derivative
f′′(x) ≈ (f(x + h) − 2f(x) + f(x − h))/h.about: Estimates curvature from three equally spaced points. It is the building block for finite-difference solutions of beam, heat, wave and Laplace equations.
assumptions: f is smooth (four times differentiable) near x; points equally spaced
Truncation error ≈ (h^{2}/12) f^{(4)}(x)
Very sensitive to noise and rounding (divides by h^{2}); don't make h too small
related: the same stencil on a grid

example.problem: Estimate the second derivative of e^{x} at x = 0 with h = 0.1.

∫ f dx ≈ (h/2)(f_{0} + 2f_{1} + 2f_{2} +.title: Trapezoid rule
∫ f dx ≈ (h/2)(f_{0} + 2f_{1} + 2f_{2} +.about: Joins the sample points with straight lines and adds up the trapezoids. It works with any number of equal intervals and with measured data, and is exact for straight lines.
assumptions: Equal spacing h = (b − a)/n; for unequal spacing sum (x_{i+1} − x_{i})(f_{i} + f_{i+1})/2 instead
Error ≈ −(b − a) h^{2} f′′/12: second order, so halving h cuts the error by four
Overestimates concave-up functions, underestimates concave-down ones
Very accurate for smooth periodic functions over a whole period

example.problem: Estimate ∫_{0}^{1} x^{2} dx with 4 intervals.
steps: Exact value 1/3: error 0.0104, an overestimate because x^{2} is concave up

∫ f dx ≈ (h/3)(f_{0} + 4f_{1} + 2f_{2} +.title: Simpson's 1/3 rule
∫ f dx ≈ (h/3)(f_{0} + 4f_{1} + 2f_{2} +.about: Fits parabolas through each pair of intervals. It is exact for cubics and fourth-order accurate, so it is far more accurate than the trapezoid rule for the same number of points.
assumptions: n must be even (an odd number of points); use Simpson's 3/8 rule on the last three intervals otherwise
Equal spacing h = (b − a)/n
Error ≈ −(b − a) h^{4} f^{(4)}/180: halving h cuts the error by 16
f must be smooth; a kink or noisy data loses most of the advantage

example.problem: Estimate ∫_{0}^{π} sin x dx with 4 intervals.
steps: Exact value 2: error 0.0046 (the trapezoid rule gives 1.896)

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n}, y_{n}).title: Euler's method for ODEs
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n}, y_{n}).about: Steps forward along the tangent line: the new value is the old one plus the step size times the current slope. It is the simplest ODE solver and the easiest to code, but only first-order accurate.
assumptions: Global error O(h): halving h only halves the error
Explicit: becomes unstable if h is too large (for y′ = λy with λ < 0 it needs h < 2/|λ|)
Fine for rough estimates and teaching; use RK4 or an adaptive solver for real work
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)
related: backward (implicit) Euler, stable for stiff problems

example.problem: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 to estimate y(0.5) for y′ = y, y(0) = 1.

k_{1} = h f(t_{n}, y_{n}).title: RK4, stage 1: slope at the start of the step
k_{1} = h f(t_{n}, y_{n}).about: The first of the four slope samples in the classical Runge–Kutta method: the plain Euler increment from the current point.
assumptions: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta: global error O(h^{4}), so halving h cuts the error about 16×
f must be smooth; jumps or discontinuities in f wreck the accuracy near them
Explicit method: for stiff systems (very fast and very slow modes together) h must stay tiny; use an implicit solver
Works the same for systems: y and each k become vectors
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)

example.problem: Take one RK4 step of h = 0.5 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1 (exact y(0.5) = e^{0.5} = 1.648721).

k_{2} = h f(t_{n} + h/2, y_{n} + k_{1}/2.title: RK4, stage 2: midpoint slope using k_{1}
k_{2} = h f(t_{n} + h/2, y_{n} + k_{1}/2.about: Use k_{1} to step half-way across the interval and sample the slope there.
assumptions: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta: global error O(h^{4}), so halving h cuts the error about 16×
f must be smooth; jumps or discontinuities in f wreck the accuracy near them
Explicit method: for stiff systems (very fast and very slow modes together) h must stay tiny; use an implicit solver
Works the same for systems: y and each k become vectors
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)

example.problem: Take one RK4 step of h = 0.5 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1 (exact y(0.5) = e^{0.5} = 1.648721).

k_{3} = h f(t_{n} + h/2, y_{n} + k_{2}/2.title: RK4, stage 3: midpoint slope again, using k_{2}
k_{3} = h f(t_{n} + h/2, y_{n} + k_{2}/2.about: A second, better midpoint sample: step half-way with the improved slope k_{2} and evaluate f again.
assumptions: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta: global error O(h^{4}), so halving h cuts the error about 16×
f must be smooth; jumps or discontinuities in f wreck the accuracy near them
Explicit method: for stiff systems (very fast and very slow modes together) h must stay tiny; use an implicit solver
Works the same for systems: y and each k become vectors
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)

example.problem: Take one RK4 step of h = 0.5 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1 (exact y(0.5) = e^{0.5} = 1.648721).

k_{4} = h f(t_{n} + h, y_{n} + k_{3}).title: RK4, stage 4: slope at the end of the step
k_{4} = h f(t_{n} + h, y_{n} + k_{3}).about: Use k_{3} to step across the whole interval and sample the slope at the far end.
assumptions: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta: global error O(h^{4}), so halving h cuts the error about 16×
f must be smooth; jumps or discontinuities in f wreck the accuracy near them
Explicit method: for stiff systems (very fast and very slow modes together) h must stay tiny; use an implicit solver
Works the same for systems: y and each k become vectors
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)

example.problem: Take one RK4 step of h = 0.5 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1 (exact y(0.5) = e^{0.5} = 1.648721).

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (k_{1} + 2k_{2} + 2k_{.title: RK4 update: weighted average of the four slopes
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (k_{1} + 2k_{2} + 2k_{.about: Combines the four stage increments with weights 1, 2, 2, 1 (Simpson's rule in time). The result matches the Taylor series through h^{4}, which is why RK4 is the workhorse fixed-step ODE solver.
assumptions: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta: global error O(h^{4}), so halving h cuts the error about 16×
f must be smooth; jumps or discontinuities in f wreck the accuracy near them
Explicit method: for stiff systems (very fast and very slow modes together) h must stay tiny; use an implicit solver
Works the same for systems: y and each k become vectors
vars: right side of y′ = f(t, y)

example.problem: Take one RK4 step of h = 0.5 for y′ = y, y(0) = 1 (exact y(0.5) = e^{0.5} = 1.648721).
steps: Error 0.00028 against e^{0.5}, compared with 0.15 for one Euler step

x = (A^{T} A)^{−1} A^{T} b.title: Least-squares solution (normal equations)
x = (A^{T} A)^{−1} A^{T} b.about: When A x = b has more equations than unknowns (more data points than parameters) there is usually no exact solution. This x minimizes the sum of squared residuals ‖A x − b‖^{2}. It is how a straight line or polynomial is fitted to data.
assumptions: A has independent columns (full column rank), so A^{T}A is invertible
Every equation is weighted equally and errors are only in b, not in A
Outliers pull the fit strongly, since errors are squared
Forming A^{T}A squares the condition number; QR or SVD is more accurate for ill-conditioned fits
related: normal equations, solved without forming the inverse
residuals, orthogonal to the columns of A
design matrix for y = c_{0} + c_{1}t

κ(A) = ‖A‖ ‖A^{−1}‖.title: Condition number of a matrix
κ(A) = ‖A‖ ‖A^{−1}‖.about: Measures how much relative errors in the data b (or in A) can be magnified in the solution of A x = b. κ near 1 is well conditioned; a large κ means the answer can lose about log_{10} κ significant digits.
assumptions: Depends on the norm used; the 2-norm gives κ = σ_{max}/σ_{min} (ratio of singular values)
κ ≥ 1 always; κ = ∞ for a singular matrix
A small determinant does not by itself mean ill conditioning (scaling changes det but not κ)
It is a worst-case bound; a particular b may fare better

example.problem: Find the 2-norm condition number of A = [1 1; 1 1.0001].
steps: About 4.6 significant digits can be lost solving A x = b

|x − x_{a}|/|x|.title: Relative error
|x − x_{a}|/|x|.about: The size of the error compared with the size of the true value. It is the right measure for comparing accuracy across quantities of different sizes, and its negative log_{10} is roughly the number of correct significant digits.
assumptions: Undefined (or meaningless) when the true value x is zero or very near it; use absolute error there
When x is unknown, the best estimate or a reference value stands in for it
Multiply by 100 for percent error

example.problem: How accurate is 22/7 as an approximation of π?

|x − x_{a}|.title: Absolute error
|x − x_{a}|.about: The size of the difference between the true value and the approximation, in the same units as the quantity. Tolerances on drawings and instrument accuracies are usually stated this way.
assumptions: Carries units, so it can't compare accuracy between quantities of very different size; use relative error for that
When the true value is unknown, compare against a more accurate reference
related: x_{a} is correct to d decimal places

example.problem: What is the absolute error of 22/7 as an approximation of π?

A = πr^{2}.title: Area of a circle
A = πr^{2}.about: The area enclosed by a circle of radius r. In engineering it is the cross-section of rods, bolts, pipes and wires, used for stress (σ = F/A) and flow (Q = vA).
assumptions: Use the radius, not the diameter; with diameter d, A = πd^{2}/4
For a tube, subtract the inner area: π(r_{o}^{2} − r_{i}^{2})

example.problem: Find the cross-sectional area of a 50 mm diameter rod.

C = 2πr.title: Circumference of a circle
C = 2πr.about: The distance around a circle. It gives wheel travel per revolution, belt lengths on pulleys and the surface speed of a rotating part (v = ωr).
assumptions: Uses the radius; with diameter C = πd
A wheel's effective rolling radius is a little less than its unloaded radius
related: arc length for part of a turn

example.problem: A wheel has a radius of 0.35 m. How far does it roll in one revolution, and how many turns per kilometre?

A = (1/2) r^{2} θ.title: Area of a circular sector
A = (1/2) r^{2} θ.about: The area of a pie slice of angle θ. It comes from the circle's area scaled by the fraction θ/(2π) of a full turn.
assumptions: θ in radians; in degrees use (θ/360°) πr^{2}
A segment (the region between chord and arc) is the sector minus the triangle: (1/2) r^{2}(θ − sin θ)
related: same area from the arc length

example.problem: Find the area of a 120° sector of radius 0.3 m.

s = rθ.title: Arc length
s = rθ.about: The length along a circle subtended by a central angle θ. This is the definition of the radian, and it links rotation to travel: a pulley turning θ moves its belt rθ.
assumptions: θ in radians; in degrees use s = (θ/360°) 2πr
Rolling without slipping assumed when used for wheels and gears

example.problem: Find the arc length of a 120° arc of radius 0.3 m.

A = πab.title: Area of an ellipse
A = πab.about: The area of an ellipse with semi-axes a and b. It reduces to πr^{2} when a = b, and appears in elliptical tanks, ducts and orbits.
assumptions: a and b are semi-axes (half the full widths)
The perimeter has no simple exact formula; Ramanujan's approximation is π(3(a + b) − √((3a + b)(a + 3b)))

example.problem: An elliptical duct is 6 m by 4 m across. Find its cross-sectional area.

A = (1/2) b h.title: Area of a triangle
A = (1/2) b h.about: Half the base times the height. The height must be perpendicular to the chosen base; any side can serve as the base.
assumptions: h is measured at right angles to b, possibly outside the triangle for an obtuse one
With three sides known use Heron's formula; with two sides and the included angle use (1/2) a b sin C
related: two sides and the included angle
centroid at h/3 from the base

example.problem: A triangular gusset plate has a 6 cm base and a 4 cm height. Find its area.

A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).title: Heron's formula
A = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).about: The area of a triangle from its three side lengths alone, with no angles or heights. Useful for surveying and for a truss panel where only the member lengths are known.
assumptions: s = (a + b + c)/2 is half the perimeter
The sides must satisfy the triangle inequality, or a factor s − a goes negative
For a very thin (needle-like) triangle it loses accuracy to rounding; sort a ≥ b ≥ c and use A = (1/4)√((a + (b + c))(c − (a − b))(c + (a − b))(a + (b − c)))
related: two sides and the angle between
law of cosines, to get the angles

example.problem: Find the area of a triangle with sides 5, 6 and 7 m.

A = (1/2) a b sin(C).title: Triangle area from two sides and the included angle
A = (1/2) a b sin(C).about: When you know two sides and the angle between them (SAS), the height on side a is b sin C, so the area is half of a × b sin C. The same expression is half the magnitude of a cross product.
assumptions: C must be the angle between sides a and b
sin is the same for C and 180° − C, so an obtuse angle works without change

example.problem: Two sides of a triangular plate are 5 cm and 7 cm with 40° between them. Find the area.

A = (1/2)(a + b) h.title: Area of a trapezoid
A = (1/2)(a + b) h.about: The average of the two parallel sides times the distance between them. It is the basis of the trapezoid rule for integration and of channel and embankment cross-sections.
assumptions: a and b are the two parallel sides
h is perpendicular to them, not the slant side

example.problem: A channel cross-section is 8 m wide at the top, 5 m at the bottom and 3 m deep. Find its area.

A = b h.title: Area of a parallelogram
A = b h.about: Base times perpendicular height; shearing a rectangle sideways doesn't change its area. It equals the magnitude of the cross product of the two edge vectors.
assumptions: h is perpendicular to the base, not the slanted side length
With side lengths and angle: A = a b sin θ
related: two sides and the angle between

example.problem: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 5 cm meeting at 30°. Find its area.

V = (4/3) πr^{3}.title: Volume of a sphere
V = (4/3) πr^{3}.about: The volume of a ball of radius r. Used for tanks, bearings, droplets and particle mass (m = ρV).
assumptions: Uses the radius; with diameter V = πd^{3}/6
Volume scales with r^{3}: doubling the radius gives 8× the volume
related: moment of inertia of a solid sphere

example.problem: Find the volume of a sphere of radius 0.1 m, and the mass if it is steel (7850 kg/m^{3}).

V = πr^{2} h.title: Volume of a cylinder
V = πr^{2} h.about: Circular base area times height. Used for tanks, pipes, hydraulic cylinders and shafts.
assumptions: A right or oblique cylinder; h is the perpendicular height
For a pipe wall use π(r_{o}^{2} − r_{i}^{2})h

example.problem: A cylindrical tank is 1 m in diameter and 2 m tall. How much does it hold?

V = (1/3) πr^{2} h.title: Volume of a cone
V = (1/3) πr^{2} h.about: One third of the cylinder with the same base and height. Used for hoppers, funnels and stockpiles.
assumptions: h is the perpendicular height from base to apex, not the slant height
For a frustum (cut-off cone) use (πh/3)(R^{2} + Rr + r^{2})
related: centroid at h/4 above the base

example.problem: A conical hopper is 0.6 m across the top and 0.9 m deep. Find its volume.

V = (1/3) B h.title: Volume of a pyramid
V = (1/3) B h.about: One third of the base area times the height, for any base shape (square, triangle, polygon). A cone is the special case with a circular base.
assumptions: h is the perpendicular height from the base plane to the apex
Works for any base shape and for an apex not directly above the centre
related: centroid at h/4 above the base

example.problem: The Great Pyramid had a square base 230 m on a side and a height of 146 m. Estimate its volume.

V = B h.title: Volume of a prism
V = B h.about: Base area times height, for any shape of constant cross-section extruded straight: beams, rods, extrusions, channels.
assumptions: The cross-section is constant along the length
h is perpendicular to the base

example.problem: A triangular-prism block has a triangular end of base 0.4 m and height 0.3 m, and is 2 m long. Find its volume.

S = 4πr^{2}.title: Surface area of a sphere
S = 4πr^{2}.about: The area of a sphere's surface: exactly four times the area of its great circle. Needed for heat loss, coating and drag estimates, and for radiation spreading over a sphere (intensity ∝ 1/(4πr^{2})).
assumptions: Uses the radius; with diameter S = πd^{2}
Surface scales as r^{2} while volume scales as r^{3}, so S/V = 3/r
related: spherical cap or zone of height h
intensity at distance r from a point source

example.problem: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 0.1 m.

S = 2πr^{2} + 2πrh.title: Surface area of a closed cylinder
S = 2πr^{2} + 2πrh.about: Two circular ends plus the curved side, which unrolls into a rectangle 2πr by h. Used for sheet-metal, paint and heat-transfer area of tanks and cans.
assumptions: Closed at both ends; drop one 2πr^{2} term for an open top, both for a tube
For the volume-optimal can (least area for a given V), h = 2r
related: minimum area for a fixed volume

example.problem: A drink can has radius 3.3 cm and height 12.2 cm. Find the area of aluminium in it.

S = πr^{2} + πr√(r^{2} + h^{2}).title: Surface area of a right circular cone
S = πr^{2} + πr√(r^{2} + h^{2}).about: The base disc plus the lateral surface πrℓ, where ℓ = √(r^{2} + h^{2}) is the slant height. The lateral part unrolls into a circular sector of radius ℓ.
assumptions: Right cone: apex directly above the centre of the base
Drop the πr^{2} term for an open cone (funnel, hopper)

example.problem: Find the total surface area of a cone with base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm.

a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}.title: Pythagorean theorem
a^{2} + b^{2} = c^{2}.about: In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. It is behind distances, vector magnitudes, resultant forces and RMS sums of perpendicular components.
assumptions: Only for right triangles (the 90° angle is opposite c); otherwise use the law of cosines
c is always the longest side
vars: the legs (sides forming the right angle)

example.problem: A 5 m ladder stands with its foot 1.4 m from a wall. How high up the wall does it reach?

c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} − 2ab cos(C).title: Law of cosines
c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} − 2ab cos(C).about: Relates the three sides of any triangle to one angle. Use it to find the third side from two sides and the included angle (SAS), or any angle from three sides (SSS). It is how force resultants and truss geometry are found.
assumptions: Any triangle; C is the angle opposite side c, between a and b
Reduces to Pythagoras when C = 90°
For an angle: cos C = (a^{2} + b^{2} − c^{2})/(2ab), always unambiguous (unlike the law of sines)
related: resultant of two forces θ apart

example.problem: Two sides of a triangle are 5 m and 7 m with 40° between them. Find the third side.

a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C).title: Law of sines
a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C).about: In any triangle each side is proportional to the sine of its opposite angle. Use it when you know two angles and a side (AAS, ASA), or two sides and a non-included angle (SSA). It is the basis of a force triangle with known directions.
assumptions: Any triangle; each angle is opposite its side
SSA case is ambiguous: sin B = x has two angles B and 180° − B, so there may be two triangles (or none)
The common ratio equals 2R, the diameter of the circumscribed circle

example.problem: In a triangle A = 40°, B = 60° and a = 10 m. Find b.

d = √((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{.title: Distance between two points
d = √((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{.about: Pythagoras applied to the coordinate differences. In 3-D add (z_{2} − z_{1})^{2}. Used for member lengths in trusses, cable lengths and position errors.
assumptions: Straight-line (Euclidean) distance in a flat, Cartesian coordinate system
Both points in the same units; on the Earth's surface over long distances use great-circle formulas
related: unit vector from point 1 to point 2

example.problem: A truss member runs from joint (1, 2) m to joint (4, 6) m. How long is it?

((x_{1} + x_{2})/2, (y_{1} + y_{2})/2).title: Midpoint of a segment
((x_{1} + x_{2})/2, (y_{1} + y_{2})/2).about: The point half-way between two points: each coordinate is the average of the two ends, since going half the distance means going half of Δx and half of Δy. It is also the centroid of a uniform rod, where its weight acts.
assumptions: Cartesian coordinates; works the same in 3-D with z
A weighted average gives the point dividing a segment in another ratio: ((1 − t)x_{1} + t x_{2}, …)
related: point a fraction t of the way along

example.problem: A uniform rod lies from (1, 2) m to (4, 6) m. Where does its weight act?

m = (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}).title: Slope of a line
m = (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}).about: Rise over run between two points. It is the rate of change of a straight-line relationship: a road grade, a calibration line's gain, the stiffness from a force-displacement plot.
assumptions: x_{1} ≠ x_{2}; a vertical line has undefined slope
For a curve this is the average rate between the two points, not the derivative at either one
The angle of the line is atan(m)
vars: slope (units of y per unit of x)

example.problem: A road rises from elevation 120 m to 132 m over a horizontal distance of 400 m. Find its slope.

x̄ = (1/n) Σ x_{i}.title: Sample mean
x̄ = (1/n) Σ x_{i}.about: The arithmetic average of n measurements: the usual best estimate of the true value or of the population mean μ. Averaging n independent readings reduces random scatter by √n.
assumptions: Measurements should be independent and from the same process
Sensitive to outliers; the median is more robust for skewed data
Averaging does not remove a systematic (bias) error

example.problem: Five length measurements are 9.8, 10.1, 10.0, 9.9 and 10.2 mm. Find the mean.

s^{2} = Σ (x_{i} − x̄)^{2} / (n − 1).title: Sample variance
s^{2} = Σ (x_{i} − x̄)^{2} / (n − 1).about: The average squared deviation from the mean, the basic measure of scatter. Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) makes it an unbiased estimate of the population variance σ^{2}, because x̄ was fitted from the same data.
assumptions: Data are a sample from a larger population; divide by n instead when you have the whole population
Units are the square of the data's units; take the square root for the standard deviation
Sensitive to outliers (deviations are squared)

example.problem: Find the sample variance of 9.8, 10.1, 10.0, 9.9, 10.2 mm.

s = √(Σ (x_{i} − x̄)^{2}/(n − 1)).title: Sample standard deviation
s = √(Σ (x_{i} − x̄)^{2}/(n − 1)).about: The square root of the variance, in the same units as the data. For roughly normal data about 68% of values fall within x̄ ± s and 95% within x̄ ± 2s.
assumptions: Same assumptions as the sample variance (n − 1 divisor)
s is a slightly biased estimate of σ even though s^{2} is unbiased; it doesn't matter for moderate n
The 68-95-99.7 rule only holds if the data are close to normal

example.problem: Find the standard deviation of 9.8, 10.1, 10.0, 9.9, 10.2 mm.

z = (x − μ)/σ.title: z-score (standardized value)
z = (x − μ)/σ.about: How many standard deviations a value lies from the mean. It turns any normal variable into the standard normal, so one table (or Φ) gives probabilities, and it flags unusual values (|z| > 3 is rare). In machine learning the same formula standardizes a feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, using the training set's μ and σ, so features on different scales weigh equally.
assumptions: μ and σ are the population values; with sample estimates and small n use the t distribution
Probabilities from z assume the data are normal

example.problem: Resistors average 1.00 kΩ with σ = 0.02 kΩ. How unusual is one measuring 1.05 kΩ?
steps: z = 2.5: only about 0.6% of resistors are that high or higher

E[X] = Σ x p(x).title: Expected value of a discrete random variable
E[X] = Σ x p(x).about: The probability-weighted average of the values X can take: the long-run mean over many trials. Used for expected cost, expected number of defects and mean load.
assumptions: Discrete X: the p(x) sum to 1; for continuous X use E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx
The expected value need not be a possible value (a die averages 3.5)

example.problem: A machined part has 0 defects with probability 0.7, 1 with 0.2 and 2 with 0.1. Find the expected number of defects.

Var(X) = E[X^{2}] − E[X]^{2}.title: Variance from moments
Var(X) = E[X^{2}] − E[X]^{2}.about: The variance equals the mean of the square minus the square of the mean. It is usually the quickest way to compute variance from a probability table or density.
assumptions: Holds for any random variable with finite variance
Prone to cancellation in floating point when the mean is large compared with the spread; use Σ(x − μ)^{2}p(x) then

example.problem: For the defect count with p(0) = 0.7, p(1) = 0.2, p(2) = 0.1, find the variance.

E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b.title: Linearity of expectation
E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b.about: Scaling and shifting a random variable scales and shifts its mean the same way. Use it for unit conversions, calibrations and linear cost models.
assumptions: a and b are constants
Holds for any distribution; no independence is needed
Only for linear functions: E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]) in general (E[X^{2}] ≠ E[X]^{2})

example.problem: A room's temperature has mean 20 °C. What is its mean in °F?

Var(aX + b) = a^{2} Var(X).title: Variance of a linear transformation
Var(aX + b) = a^{2} Var(X).about: Shifting a variable doesn't change its spread; scaling by a multiplies the variance by a^{2} (and the standard deviation by |a|).
assumptions: a and b are constants
Holds for any distribution

example.problem: A temperature has standard deviation 2 °C (variance 4 °C^{2}). Find its variance in °F.

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).title: Addition rule for probabilities
P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).about: The probability that A or B (or both) happens. The overlap is subtracted because adding P(A) and P(B) counts it twice.
assumptions: Holds for any two events
For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0 and it reduces to P(A) + P(B)
For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
related: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣP − ΣP(pairs) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C)

example.problem: A part has a scratch with probability 0.3, a dent with 0.2, and both with 0.05. What is the chance it has at least one flaw?

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).title: Conditional probability
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).about: The probability of A given that B is known to have happened: restrict attention to the outcomes where B is true. It is the basis of reliability given a symptom and of Bayes' rule.
assumptions: A and B are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A)
P(A | B) and P(B | A) are generally different; mixing them up is a classic error

example.problem: A part has a dent with probability 0.2 and both a dent and a scratch with probability 0.05. Given it has a dent, what is the chance it is also scratched?

P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A)/P(B).title: Bayes' theorem
P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A)/P(B).about: Reverses a conditional probability: from how likely the evidence is under a hypothesis to how likely the hypothesis is given the evidence. It explains why a positive result on a good test for a rare condition is often a false alarm.
assumptions: P(B) > 0, usually found by total probability: P(B) = P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | A^{c})P(A^{c})
The prior P(A) matters a lot when it is small (base-rate effect)
vars: posterior: probability of A after seeing B
likelihood of B if A is true

example.problem: A fault affects 1% of units. A test catches 99% of faulty units but also flags 5% of good ones. If a unit is flagged, how likely is it faulty?
steps: Only 1 in 6 flagged units is actually faulty

nPr = n!/(n − r)!.title: Permutations: ordered selections
nPr = n!/(n − r)!.about: The number of ways to pick r items from n distinct items when the order matters (first, second, third…): a podium, a sequence of operations, a code with no repeated digits.
assumptions: Items are distinct and each is used at most once (no repetition)
With repetition allowed the count is n^{r}
0! = 1, so nPn = n!
vars: number of items to choose from

example.problem: Ten runners compete. How many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded?

nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!).title: Combinations: unordered selections
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!).about: The number of ways to choose r items from n distinct items when order doesn't matter: a committee, a sample of parts, a hand of cards. It is also the binomial coefficient in (a + b)^{n}.
assumptions: Items are distinct and each is used at most once
nCr = nC(n − r)
nCr = nPr/r!, since each unordered group can be ordered r! ways
vars: number of items to choose from

example.problem: How many different 5-card hands can be dealt from a 52-card deck?

Binomial ‖ nCk p^{k} (1 − p)^{n−k} ‖ np,.title: Binomial distribution
Binomial ‖ nCk p^{k} (1 − p)^{n−k} ‖ np,.about: The probability of exactly k successes in n independent trials, each succeeding with probability p. Used for defective parts in a batch, pass/fail tests and acceptance sampling.
assumptions: A fixed number n of trials
Each trial is independent with the same probability p
Only two outcomes per trial
Sampling without replacement from a small lot breaks independence (use hypergeometric)
For large n and small p it approaches Poisson with λ = np
related: approximation for large n, small p

example.problem: 5% of parts are defective. In a sample of 10, what is the chance of exactly one defective?

Poisson ‖ λ^{k} e^{−λ}/k! ‖ λ, λ.title: Poisson distribution
Poisson ‖ λ^{k} e^{−λ}/k! ‖ λ, λ.about: The probability of k events in a fixed interval when events happen independently at a constant average rate. Used for arrivals, failures, defects per area and radioactive counts.
assumptions: Events are independent and occur one at a time
The average rate is constant over the interval
λ is the mean count for the whole interval (rate × time)
Mean equals variance; if the data's variance is much larger, the model is wrong (over-dispersion)
vars: mean number of events in the interval
related: Binomial n, p → Poisson λ = np

example.problem: A help desk gets an average of 3 calls per minute. What is the probability of exactly 5 calls in a minute?

Geometric ‖ (1 − p)^{k−1} p ‖ 1/p, (1 −.title: Geometric distribution
Geometric ‖ (1 − p)^{k−1} p ‖ 1/p, (1 −.about: The probability that the first success happens on trial k, after k − 1 failures. Used for the number of attempts until a connection succeeds, a part fails, or a test passes.
assumptions: Independent trials with the same success probability p
Here k counts the trial of the first success (k = 1, 2, …); some texts count failures instead, which shifts the mean to (1 − p)/p
Memoryless: past failures don't change the chance of success on the next trial
vars: trial on which the first success occurs

example.problem: Each attempt to start an engine succeeds with probability 0.2. What is the chance the first success is on the third attempt?

Uniform ‖ 1/(b − a) ‖ (a + b)/2, (b − a).title: Continuous uniform distribution
Uniform ‖ 1/(b − a) ‖ (a + b)/2, (b − a).about: Every value between a and b is equally likely. It models rounding and quantization error, a random phase, or a quantity known only to lie within limits. The probability of an interval is its length over b − a.
assumptions: X is continuous and confined to [a, b], with constant density there
Quantization error of step Δ is uniform on ±Δ/2, so its standard deviation is Δ/√12

example.problem: A delay is uniform between 2 and 8 ms. Find the chance it is at most 3.5 ms, and its mean and variance.

Exponential ‖ λ e^{−λx} ‖ 1/λ, 1/λ^{2}.title: Exponential distribution
Exponential ‖ λ e^{−λx} ‖ 1/λ, 1/λ^{2}.about: The waiting time between events of a Poisson process, and the lifetime of a part with a constant failure rate. The chance of surviving past x is e^{−λx}.
assumptions: Constant rate λ: no wear-out and no infant mortality (use Weibull otherwise)
Memoryless: a unit that has survived so far is as good as new
x ≥ 0; λ is the rate, 1/λ the mean (MTBF)
vars: rate (failures or events per unit time)

example.problem: A pump has a mean time between failures of 1000 h. What is the chance it runs 500 h without failing?

Normal ‖ e^{−(x − μ)^{2}/(2σ^{2})} / (σ√.title: Normal (Gaussian) distribution
Normal ‖ e^{−(x − μ)^{2}/(2σ^{2})} / (σ√.about: The bell curve. Sums and averages of many small independent effects tend toward it (central limit theorem), so it models measurement error, manufacturing variation and noise. Probabilities come from areas under the curve, through z = (x − μ)/σ.
assumptions: Symmetric, unbounded tails; a quantity that can't be negative or is strongly skewed may fit poorly
The density value is not a probability; integrate it over an interval (or use Φ)
Real data often have heavier tails than normal, so extreme events are underestimated

example.problem: A quantity is normal with μ = 100 and σ = 15. Find the density at x = 115.

x̄ ± z σ/√n.title: Confidence interval for a mean
x̄ ± z σ/√n.about: A range that captures the true mean μ with the chosen confidence (for example 95% of such intervals contain μ). The half-width z σ/√n is the margin of error; it shrinks with more samples as 1/√n.
assumptions: σ is known, or n is large (about 30+) so s can stand in for σ; for small n with s use t instead of z
Observations are independent and either normal or numerous enough for the central limit theorem
It covers random error only, not bias in the measurement
vars: critical value for the confidence level
related: sample size for a margin E

example.problem: 25 measurements average 50.2 mm and σ = 1.5 mm is known. Find the 95% confidence interval for the mean.

z = 1.645.title: Critical z for 90% confidence
z = 1.645.about: The standard normal value with 5% of the area beyond it in each tail, so 90% lies between −1.645 and +1.645. It is also the critical value for a one-sided test at 5% significance.
assumptions: Assumes the statistic is (approximately) normal
Two-sided 90%, or one-sided 95%
With a small sample and an estimated σ, use the t value, which is larger

example.problem: 16 readings average 30.0 with σ = 4. Find the 90% confidence interval.

z = 1.960.title: Critical z for 95% confidence
z = 1.960.about: The standard normal value with 2.5% in each tail, so 95% of the area lies within ±1.96. It is the most common confidence level and the two-sided 5% significance threshold.
assumptions: Assumes the statistic is (approximately) normal
Two-sided 95%; one-sided 97.5%
Often rounded to 2, which is the 95.45% (2σ) level
related: sample size for a margin E

example.problem: σ = 2 mm. How many samples are needed for a 95% margin of error of 0.5 mm?

z = 2.576.title: Critical z for 99% confidence
z = 2.576.about: The standard normal value with 0.5% in each tail, so 99% of the area lies within ±2.576. Used when a missed effect would be costly.
assumptions: Assumes the statistic is (approximately) normal
Two-sided 99%; one-sided 99.5%
Higher confidence means a wider interval for the same data

example.problem: Nine readings average 12.0 with σ = 0.3. Find the 99% confidence interval.

within 1σ: 68.27%.title: Normal curve: share within one standard deviation
within 1σ: 68.27%.about: For normally distributed data, 68.27% of values lie within μ ± σ, so about one value in three falls outside.
assumptions: Only for a normal distribution; for any distribution Chebyshev guarantees only that at least 1 − 1/k^{2} lies within kσ
Equals erf(1/√2) = 2Φ(1) − 1

example.problem: Shaft diameters are normal with μ = 50.0 mm and σ = 0.1 mm. What fraction lie between 49.9 and 50.1 mm?

within 2σ: 95.45%.title: Normal curve: share within two standard deviations
within 2σ: 95.45%.about: For normally distributed data, 95.45% of values lie within μ ± 2σ. This is why ±2σ is used as a rough 95% band (the exact 95% value is 1.96σ).
assumptions: Only for a normal distribution
Equals erf(2/√2) = 2Φ(2) − 1

example.problem: With μ = 50.0 mm and σ = 0.1 mm, what fraction of shafts lie between 49.8 and 50.2 mm?

within 3σ: 99.73%.title: Normal curve: share within three standard deviations
within 3σ: 99.73%.about: For normally distributed data, 99.73% of values lie within μ ± 3σ: only about 27 in 10 000 fall outside. Control charts use ±3σ limits, and process capability is judged against them.
assumptions: Only for a normal distribution; real processes often have heavier tails, so more fall outside
Equals erf(3/√2) = 2Φ(3) − 1

example.problem: A process makes 10 000 parts with tolerance limits at μ ± 3σ. About how many are out of tolerance?

det A = ad − bc.title: Determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix
det A = ad − bc.about: The product of the main diagonal minus the product of the other diagonal. It is zero exactly when the matrix is singular (no inverse, no unique solution of A x = b), and |det A| is the area scale factor of the transformation.
assumptions: A is square; here A = [a b; c d]
det A = 0: columns are parallel (dependent); the system has no or infinitely many solutions
A sign change means the transformation flips orientation
related: Cramer's rule for ax + by = e, cx + dy = f

example.problem: Find the determinant of A = [4 3; 6 3].

A^{−1} = (1/det A) [d −b; −c a].title: Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
A^{−1} = (1/det A) [d −b; −c a].about: Swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones, and divide by the determinant. Then x = A^{−1} b solves A x = b, though for computation solving directly is usually better than inverting.
assumptions: det A = ad − bc ≠ 0
A nearly singular matrix (det small relative to its entries) gives a large, error-sensitive inverse
Check: A A^{−1} = I

example.problem: Invert A = [4 7; 2 6].

det A = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh −.title: Determinant of a 3 × 3 matrix (cofactor expansion)
det A = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh −.about: Expand along the first row: each entry times the determinant of the 2 × 2 matrix left when its row and column are removed, with signs + − +. |det A| is the volume scale factor; zero means singular.
assumptions: A = [a b c; d e f; g h i]
Any row or column can be used, with the checkerboard sign pattern; pick one with zeros to save work
For larger matrices use row reduction: det = product of the pivots (times −1 per row swap)
related: det A = aei + bfg + cdh − ceg − bdi − afh
scalar triple product of the rows

example.problem: Find the determinant of A = [2 1 3; 0 4 1; 5 2 0].

(AB)^{T} = B^{T} A^{T}.title: Transpose of a product
(AB)^{T} = B^{T} A^{T}.about: The transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in reverse order. The reversal is needed for the dimensions to match, and it shows up in stiffness matrices (K = B^{T} D B) and least squares.
assumptions: A is m × n and B is n × p, so AB is defined
Order reverses; A^{T} B^{T} is generally a different matrix or not even defined
Extends to more factors: (ABC)^{T} = C^{T} B^{T} A^{T}

example.problem: A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 4. Check that the dimensions work, and verify the rule for A = [1 2], B = [3; 4] (a 1 × 2 times a 2 × 1).
steps: B^{T} is 4 × 3 and A^{T} is 3 × 2, so B^{T} A^{T} is 4 × 2 ✓ (A^{T} B^{T} would be 3 × 2 times 4 × 3: undefined)
example.answer: (AB)^{T} is 4 × 2 = B^{T} A^{T}; both equal 11 in the small case

(AB)^{−1} = B^{−1} A^{−1}.title: Inverse of a product
(AB)^{−1} = B^{−1} A^{−1}.about: In AB x, B acts on x first and A second, so undoing the product means undoing A first and then B, the same way shoes come off before socks.
assumptions: A and B are square and both invertible (det ≠ 0)
Order reverses; A^{−1} B^{−1} is wrong unless A and B commute
related: so AB is invertible iff both are

example.problem: With A = [2 0; 0 1] and B = [1 1; 0 1], find (AB)^{−1} both ways.

det(AB) = det(A) det(B).title: Determinant of a product
det(AB) = det(A) det(B).about: Area or volume scale factors multiply when transformations are combined. A product is singular if either factor is.
assumptions: A and B are square and the same size
There is no such rule for sums: det(A + B) ≠ det(A) + det(B) in general
vars: square matrices of the same size

example.problem: A = [2 1; 0 1] has det 2 and B = [3 0; 1 1] has det 3. Find det(AB).

det(A^{T}) = det(A).title: Determinant of a transpose
det(A^{T}) = det(A).about: Transposing doesn't change the determinant, so everything true about rows of a determinant is also true about columns (swapping, scaling, adding multiples).
assumptions: A is square
related: det(A) = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg)

example.problem: Check the rule for A = [4 3; 6 3].

det(A^{−1}) = 1/det(A).title: Determinant of an inverse
det(A^{−1}) = 1/det(A).about: If A scales areas or volumes by det A, its inverse must scale them back by 1/det A. It follows from det(A) det(A^{−1}) = det(I) = 1.
assumptions: A is square and invertible (det A ≠ 0)
A tiny det A means a huge det(A^{−1}), a hint (not proof) of an ill-conditioned matrix

a · b = Σ a_{i} b_{i} = |a| |b| cos(θ).title: Dot product
a · b = Σ a_{i} b_{i} = |a| |b| cos(θ).about: Multiply matching components and add. It equals the product of the lengths times the cosine of the angle between them, so it gives angles between vectors, work done by a force (W = F · d) and tests for perpendicularity (a · b = 0).
assumptions: Both vectors have the same number of components, in the same coordinate system
The result is a scalar
θ is between 0 and 180°; a negative dot product means θ > 90°

example.problem: Find the angle between a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (3, 0, 4).

|a × b| = |a| |b| sin(θ).title: Magnitude of the cross product
|a × b| = |a| |b| sin(θ).about: The length of a × b equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b. In mechanics it gives the size of a moment (|r × F| = rF sin θ) and of the force on a current in a magnetic field.
assumptions: 3-D vectors
θ is the angle between the vectors (0 to 180°); parallel vectors give zero
Only the perpendicular part of F produces a moment: r F sin θ = r F_{⊥}

example.problem: A 40 N force acts at the end of a 0.25 m wrench, at 60° to the handle. Find the moment about the bolt.

a × b = (a_{2}b_{3} − a_{3}b_{2}, a_{3}b.title: Cross product in components
a × b = (a_{2}b_{3} − a_{3}b_{2}, a_{3}b.about: A vector perpendicular to both a and b, with direction from the right-hand rule and length |a||b| sin θ. Used for moments (M = r × F), normals to surfaces, angular velocity (v = ω × r) and magnetic force.
assumptions: 3-D vectors only
Not commutative: b × a = −(a × b)
Right-handed coordinate system (x × y = z)

example.problem: Find a × b for a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (4, 5, 6).

|a| = √(a · a).title: Length (magnitude) of a vector
|a| = √(a · a).about: The square root of the sum of the squared components: Pythagoras in any number of dimensions. Gives the size of a force, velocity or displacement, and dividing by it gives a unit vector.
assumptions: Cartesian (orthonormal) components
All components in the same units

example.problem: A force is F = (3, 4, 12) N. Find its magnitude.

proj_{b} a = ((a · b)/(b · b)) b.title: Vector projection
proj_{b} a = ((a · b)/(b · b)) b.about: The component of a that points along b, as a vector. Used to resolve a force along and across an incline or a member, and it is the idea behind least squares (the closest point on a line).
assumptions: The scalar projection (signed length) is (a · b)/|b|
a − proj_{b} a is the part of a perpendicular to b

example.problem: A force F = (30, 40) N acts on a slider whose track runs along b = (4, 3). Find the force component along the track.

A v = λ v.title: Eigenvalue equation
A v = λ v.about: An eigenvector v is a direction that A only stretches, by the factor λ. Eigenvalues give natural frequencies and mode shapes in vibration, principal stresses and axes, stability of x′ = A x, and growth rates of iterated systems.
assumptions: A is square; v ≠ 0
An n × n matrix has n eigenvalues counting repeats, possibly complex
Real symmetric matrices (stress tensors, stiffness) have real eigenvalues and perpendicular eigenvectors
Eigenvectors are defined only up to scale
related: tr(A) = Σ λ_{i}, det(A) = Π λ_{i}
modal solution of x′ = A x

example.problem: Show that v = (1, 1) is an eigenvector of A = [2 1; 1 2] and find its eigenvalue.

det(A − λI) = 0.title: Characteristic equation for eigenvalues
det(A − λI) = 0.about: A v = λ v has a nonzero solution only when A − λI is singular. Setting its determinant to zero gives a polynomial whose roots are the eigenvalues.
assumptions: A is n × n, giving a degree-n polynomial
For 2 × 2: λ^{2} − tr(A) λ + det(A) = 0
By hand only for small matrices; numerically use the QR algorithm (the polynomial's roots are ill-conditioned)

example.problem: Find the eigenvalues of A = [2 1; 1 2].

tr(A) = Σ λ_{i}.title: Trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues
tr(A) = Σ λ_{i}.about: The sum of the diagonal entries equals the sum of the eigenvalues (with repeats). It is a fast check on computed eigenvalues, and for a stress tensor it is the first invariant (σ_{1} + σ_{2} + σ_{3}).
assumptions: A is square; complex eigenvalues are included and come in conjugate pairs for real A
vars: trace: sum of the diagonal entries

example.problem: A = [4 1; 2 3]. Find its eigenvalues and check the trace.

det(A) = Π λ_{i}.title: Determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues
det(A) = Π λ_{i}.about: The determinant is the product of all eigenvalues. So a matrix is singular exactly when it has a zero eigenvalue, and this is a quick check on computed eigenvalues.
assumptions: A is square; include repeated and complex eigenvalues

example.problem: A = [4 1; 2 3] has eigenvalues 2 and 5. Check the determinant.

A = l w.title: Area of a rectangle
A = l w.about: Length times width: the area of any rectangle, and of anything built from rectangles (floor plans, plates, rectangular cross-sections of beams).
assumptions: Both sides in the same unit; the area comes out in that unit squared
Every corner is a right angle; a slanted (sheared) shape is a parallelogram, A = b h
related: second moment of area of a rectangular section

example.problem: A room is 4.2 m by 3.5 m. Find its floor area.

P = 2(l + w).title: Perimeter of a rectangle
P = 2(l + w).about: The distance around a rectangle: two lengths plus two widths. Use it for fencing, edging, weld length around a plate or the wetted perimeter of a rectangular duct.
assumptions: Both sides in the same unit

example.problem: How much fence surrounds a 12 m by 8 m yard?

A = (√3/4) a^{2}.title: Area of an equilateral triangle
A = (√3/4) a^{2}.about: The area of a triangle with three equal sides a. It is half base times height, with the height (√3/2)a from Pythagoras on half the triangle.
assumptions: All three sides equal (all angles 60°); otherwise use (1/2) b h or Heron

example.problem: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm.

A = (1/4) n s^{2} cot(π/n).title: Area of a regular polygon
A = (1/4) n s^{2} cot(π/n).about: The area of a regular polygon with n equal sides of length s. It splits into n identical isosceles triangles meeting at the centre, each of base s and height (s/2) cot(π/n), the apothem.
assumptions: Regular: all sides and all angles equal
π/n in radians (or 180°/n in degrees)
related: apothem (centre to the middle of a side)
half the perimeter times the apothem

example.problem: Find the area of a regular hexagon of side 2 m.

V = l w h.title: Volume of a box (rectangular prism)
V = l w h.about: Length times width times height: the volume of a rectangular block, tank or room. 1 m^{3} = 1000 L.
assumptions: All faces rectangular, every corner a right angle
All three edges in the same unit
related: S = 2(l w + l h + w h)

example.problem: A tank is 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m. How many litres does it hold?

S = 2(l w + l h + w h).title: Surface area of a box
S = 2(l w + l h + w h).about: The total area of a box's six rectangular faces, which come in three equal pairs. Use it for sheet metal, paint, insulation and heat loss from a rectangular enclosure.
assumptions: A closed box; drop one l w term for an open top
All three edges in the same unit

example.problem: Find the surface area of a 3 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm box.

A + B + C = 180°.title: Angle sum of a triangle
A + B + C = 180°.about: The three interior angles of any flat triangle add to 180° (π rad). Use it to find the third angle before applying the law of sines, or to check a force triangle.
assumptions: A flat (Euclidean) triangle; on a sphere the sum exceeds 180°
The angles are interior angles
related: exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles

example.problem: Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 65°. Find the third.

1 : 1 : √2.title: 45-45-90 triangle
1 : 1 : √2.about: The side ratio of an isosceles right triangle: two equal legs and a hypotenuse √2 times a leg. It is half a square cut along its diagonal, and gives sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 exactly.
assumptions: Angles 45°, 45° and 90°
vars: each of the two equal sides
related: diagonal of a square of side s

example.problem: The legs of a right isosceles triangle are 5 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

1 : √3 : 2.title: 30-60-90 triangle
1 : √3 : 2.about: The side ratio of a right triangle with angles 30° and 60°: short leg (opposite 30°), long leg √3 times it, hypotenuse twice it. It is half an equilateral triangle, and gives the exact sin and cos of 30° and 60°.
assumptions: Angles 30°, 60° and 90°
The short leg is opposite the 30° angle

example.problem: The hypotenuse of a 30-60-90 triangle is 10 cm. Find both legs.

(n − 2) 180°.title: Sum of the interior angles of a polygon
(n − 2) 180°.about: The interior angles of any simple n-sided polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°, because diagonals from one vertex split it into n − 2 triangles. For a regular polygon each angle is that sum divided by n.
assumptions: A simple polygon (sides don't cross); it may be convex or not
related: each angle of a regular n-gon
sum of the exterior angles, any n

example.problem: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.

d = √((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{.title: Distance between two points in 3D
d = √((x_{2} − x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} − y_{.about: The straight-line distance between two points in space: Pythagoras applied twice. Use it for the length of a space-truss member, a cable between two anchors, or the size of a position vector.
assumptions: Cartesian coordinates, all in the same unit

example.problem: A cable runs from (1, 2, 3) m to (4, 6, 15) m. How long is it?

d = (|a x_{0} + b y_{0} + c|)/√(a^{2} +.title: Distance from a point to a line
d = (|a x_{0} + b y_{0} + c|)/√(a^{2} +.about: The shortest (perpendicular) distance from the point (x_{0}, y_{0}) to the line ax + by + c = 0. Use it for clearances, the moment arm of a force about a point, or the error of a point from a fitted line.
assumptions: The line must be written as ax + by + c = 0 first (y = mx + k becomes mx − y + k = 0)
a and b not both zero
Without the absolute value the sign tells which side of the line the point is on
vars: coefficients of the line ax + by + c = 0
related: moment of a force with arm d

example.problem: Find the distance from (1, 2) to the line 3x + 4y − 1 = 0.

σ^{2} = Σ (x_{i} − μ)^{2}/N.title: Population variance
σ^{2} = Σ (x_{i} − μ)^{2}/N.about: The mean squared distance from the mean when you have every member of the population (or a theoretical distribution). Divide by N, not n − 1: no correction is needed because μ is the true mean, not one estimated from the same data.
assumptions: The data are the whole population; for a sample use s^{2} with n − 1
Units are the data's units squared; σ = √(σ^{2})

example.problem: A population is 2, 4, 6. Find its variance.

σ_{x̄} = σ/√n.title: Standard error of the mean
σ_{x̄} = σ/√n.about: How much the mean of n independent readings varies from sample to sample: the standard deviation of x̄. Averaging more readings narrows it as 1/√n, so quadrupling n halves it. It is the scale for confidence intervals and z or t tests on a mean.
assumptions: Readings independent and from the same distribution
With σ unknown use s in its place (then intervals use t)
It shrinks random error only, not a systematic bias
vars: standard deviation of a single reading (s if σ is unknown)
related: sample size for a margin E

example.problem: Single readings scatter with σ = 12. What is the standard error of the mean of 36 readings?

σ_{XY} = E[XY] − E[X] E[Y].title: Covariance
σ_{XY} = E[XY] − E[X] E[Y].about: How two variables move together: positive when they tend to rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls, zero when independent. It is the term that makes the variance of a sum differ from the sum of the variances.
assumptions: Independent X and Y have σ_{XY} = 0, but zero covariance does not prove independence (only no linear relation)
Its size depends on the units; for a unit-free measure use r = σ_{XY}/(σ_{X} σ_{Y})
From a sample: s_{xy} = Σ (x_{i} − x̄)(y_{i} − ȳ)/(n − 1)

example.problem: E[XY] = 10, E[X] = 2 and E[Y] = 3. Find Cov(X, Y).

r = σ_{XY}/(σ_{X} σ_{Y}).title: Correlation coefficient (Pearson r)
r = σ_{XY}/(σ_{X} σ_{Y}).about: Covariance scaled to between −1 and 1: the strength and direction of a straight-line relationship. r = ±1 means the points lie exactly on a line; r = 0 means no linear trend. r^{2} is the share of the variance in y explained by a line in x.
assumptions: Measures linear association only: a perfect curve (y = x^{2} on symmetric x) can give r = 0
Sensitive to outliers
Correlation is not causation
vars: standard deviations of X and Y

example.problem: Cov(X, Y) = 4, σ_{X} = 2 and σ_{Y} = 5. Find r.

b_{1} = r s_{y}/s_{x}.title: Least-squares regression slope
b_{1} = r s_{y}/s_{x}.about: The slope of the least-squares line ŷ = b_{0} + b_{1}x. A point one standard deviation above x̄ is predicted only r standard deviations above ȳ; the factor s_{y}/s_{x} turns those standard units into y-units per x-unit. Since |r| ≤ 1, predictions ‘regress toward the mean’.
assumptions: Minimises the vertical squared errors; regressing x on y gives a different line, not this one inverted
Fits a straight-line trend only: check the residuals for a curve
Don’t extrapolate far beyond the range of x in the data
vars: units of y per unit of x
standard deviations of x and y
related: intercept: the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
variance explained, r^{2} for one feature

example.problem: Hours studied (s_{x} = 2 h) and exam score (s_{y} = 5 points) have r = 0.8. Find the regression slope.

b_{0} = ȳ − b_{1} x̄.title: Least-squares regression intercept
b_{0} = ȳ − b_{1} x̄.about: The intercept of the least-squares line ŷ = b_{0} + b_{1}x. The best-fit line always passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ), which fixes b_{0} once the slope is known.
assumptions: Find the slope b_{1} first (b_{1} = r s_{y}/s_{x})
The intercept may be meaningless if x = 0 lies far outside the data

example.problem: Data have x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 10, and the fitted slope is b_{1} = 2. Find the intercept.

E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx.title: Expected value of a continuous random variable
E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx.about: The probability-weighted average of a continuous variable: the mean, with the density f(x) in place of the discrete probabilities. It is the balance point of the density curve.
assumptions: f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over the whole range
Integrate over every x where f is non-zero
Some heavy-tailed densities (Cauchy) have no mean

example.problem: X is uniform on [0, 4]. Find E[X].

Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2σ_{XY}.title: Variance of a sum
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2σ_{XY}.about: The spread of a sum of two random quantities, such as stacked tolerances or two noise sources. For independent variables the variances add (standard deviations add in quadrature); correlation adds twice the covariance.
assumptions: Holds for any X and Y; σ_{XY} = 0 when they are independent
For a difference: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2σ_{XY}
Add variances, never standard deviations

example.problem: Two independent parts stack end to end; their lengths have variances 4 mm^{2} and 9 mm^{2}. Find the standard deviation of the total length.

P(A^{c}) = 1 − P(A).title: Complement rule
P(A^{c}) = 1 − P(A).about: A and ‘not A’ cover every outcome without overlapping, so their probabilities add to 1. It turns a hard ‘at least one’ question into an easy ‘none at all’ one: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
assumptions: A^{c} is every outcome not in A
For n independent trials P(none) = (1 − p)^{n}; adding the single-trial chances instead is a classic mistake (4 × 1/6 = 0.667 is wrong)
vars: probability that A does not happen
related: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
at least one success in n trials

example.problem: A die is rolled 4 times. What is the chance of at least one six?

P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B).title: Multiplication rule for independent events
P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B).about: When knowing one event tells you nothing about the other, the chance that both happen is the product. It gives the reliability of components in series and the chance of repeated independent outcomes.
assumptions: A and B independent; otherwise P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) P(B)
Not the same as mutually exclusive: exclusive events with non-zero probability are never independent
related: reliability of independent parts in series

example.problem: Two independent pumps are each available 95% of the time. What is the chance both are available?

P(B) = Σ P(B | A_{i}) P(A_{i}).title: Law of total probability
P(B) = Σ P(B | A_{i}) P(A_{i}).about: To get the overall chance of B, split the outcomes into cases A_{i}, find B’s chance within each case, and average those chances weighted by how likely each case is. It is the denominator of Bayes’ theorem.
assumptions: The A_{i} don’t overlap and together cover everything (Σ P(A_{i}) = 1); the two-case form uses A and A^{c}
Leaving out a case, such as the healthy people who test positive, is the usual mistake
vars: probability of B within case i
related: Bayes’ theorem, which divides by it

example.problem: 1% of people have a disease. A test detects 99% of cases and false-alarms on 5% of healthy people. What fraction of all tests are positive?

x̄ ± t s/√n.title: Confidence interval for a mean (t interval)
x̄ ± t s/√n.about: The interval for a mean when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample s. The t value, with n − 1 degrees of freedom, is larger than z to allow for the extra uncertainty in s; it approaches z as n grows.
assumptions: Data roughly normal, or n large enough (about 30+) for the central limit theorem
Observations independent
Read t from a table for n − 1 degrees of freedom and the confidence level (two-sided)
vars: critical t value, n − 1 degrees of freedom

example.problem: 16 measurements have mean 50 and s = 8. Find the 95% confidence interval (t = 2.131 for 15 df).

p̂ ± z √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).title: Confidence interval for a proportion
p̂ ± z √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).about: The range likely to hold the true population proportion p, from a sample proportion p̂ = x/n. A yes/no answer has standard deviation √(p(1 − p)), so p̂ has standard error √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n), and the margin is z of those. It is the ‘± 3%’ quoted with polls.
assumptions: n p̂ and n(1 − p̂) both at least about 10, so p̂ is close to normal; otherwise use the Wilson interval
A random sample with independent responses
The margin is widest at p̂ = 0.5, so plans assume p̂ = 0.5 when nothing is known
related: sample size, with σ^{2} = p(1 − p)

example.problem: In a survey, 420 of 1000 people say yes. Find the 95% confidence interval for the true proportion.

n = (z σ/E)^{2}.title: Sample size for a margin of error
n = (z σ/E)^{2}.about: How many samples make a confidence interval for a mean ±E wide: the margin E = zσ/√n solved for n. Because n goes as 1/E^{2}, halving the margin takes four times the samples.
assumptions: Always round up to the next whole sample, even 96.04 → 97
σ must be known or estimated beforehand (a pilot run or past data)
For a proportion use σ^{2} = p(1 − p), with p = 0.5 when unknown

example.problem: Part lengths scatter with σ = 15 mm. How many parts must be measured to know the mean within ±3 mm at 95% confidence?

z = (x̄ − μ_{0})/(σ/√n).title: z test statistic for a mean
z = (x̄ − μ_{0})/(σ/√n).about: How many standard errors the sample mean lies from a hypothesised mean μ_{0}. Compare |z| with the critical value (1.96 for a two-sided test at 5%); larger means the difference is unlikely to be chance.
assumptions: σ known (or n large); with s and small n use the t statistic
Observations independent, data normal or n large
A one-sided test uses 1.645 at 5%

example.problem: A process should average μ_{0} = 100 with σ = 15. A sample of 25 averages 106. Is that a significant shift at 5% (two-sided)?

t = (x̄ − μ_{0})/(s/√n).title: One-sample t statistic
t = (x̄ − μ_{0})/(s/√n).about: How many standard errors the sample mean lies from the hypothesised mean μ_{0}, using the sample’s own s in place of σ. Because s is itself uncertain, compare with the t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, whose critical values exceed z’s for small n.
assumptions: Roughly normal data, or n large (about 30+)
Independent observations
σ unknown; if it is known, use z
Choose one- or two-sided before seeing the data: the critical values differ

example.problem: Nine bolts have mean 52 N·m and s = 6 N·m. Is that above the 48 N·m spec at 5% (t critical 1.860 one-sided, 8 df)?

(AB)_{ij} = Σ_{k} a_{ik} b_{kj}.title: Matrix multiplication
(AB)_{ij} = Σ_{k} a_{ik} b_{kj}.about: Entry (i, j) is row i of A dotted with column j of B. A must have as many columns as B has rows. A common mistake is assuming AB = BA.
assumptions: A is m × n and B is n × p; AB is m × p
Not commutative: AB ≠ BA in general

example.problem: Multiply [1 2; 3 4] by [5; 6].

A A^{−1} = A^{−1} A = I.title: Matrix inverse
A A^{−1} = A^{−1} A = I.about: The inverse undoes A, from either side. It exists only for a square A with det A ≠ 0; a zero determinant means A squashes some direction to zero, which can't be undone. A common mistake is inverting entry by entry; that works only for a diagonal matrix.
assumptions: A is square
det A ≠ 0; otherwise A is singular and has no inverse

example.problem: Find and check [2 0; 0 4]^{−1}.
steps: A diagonal matrix inverts entry by entry: [1/2 0; 0 1/4]

x = A^{−1} b.title: Solving a linear system with the inverse
x = A^{−1} b.about: Multiply both sides of A x = b on the left by A^{−1}: A^{−1}A = I leaves x. For square, invertible A there is exactly one solution. A common mistake is b A^{−1}; the inverse must go on the left, as matrix products don't commute.
assumptions: A square with det A ≠ 0
For large systems, elimination (LU) is faster and more accurate than forming A^{−1}

example.problem: Solve 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10.

x_{i} = det(A_{i})/det(A).title: Cramer's rule
x_{i} = det(A_{i})/det(A).about: Each unknown is a ratio of determinants; handy for 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 by hand. A common mistake is replacing a row of A with b; it is column i.
assumptions: A square with det A ≠ 0
Practical by hand for 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 only
vars: A with column i replaced by b
related: the same solution by the inverse

example.problem: Solve 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10 for x.

det(cA) = c^{n} det(A).title: Determinant of a scaled matrix
