det(cA) = c^{n} det(A).about: Scaling multiplies every row by c, and each row scales det by c. A common mistake is c det(A); each of the n rows carries a factor c.
assumptions: A is square, n × n
c multiplies each of the n rows, and each row scales det by c

example.problem: det A = 3 for a 3 × 3 A. Find det(2A).

A^{T} = A.title: Symmetric matrix
A^{T} = A.about: Equal to its own transpose. Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. A common mistake is expecting a non-symmetric matrix to have real eigenvalues; it may not.
assumptions: A square
Stiffness, mass and inertia matrices, and every A^{T}A, are symmetric
related: its eigenvectors form an orthogonal Q

example.problem: Is [1 2; 2 5] symmetric, and are its eigenvalues real?
steps: Its transpose is itself, so yes

Q^{T} Q = I.title: Orthogonal matrix
Q^{T} Q = I.about: Q^{T}Q lists every dot product of Q's columns; it is I exactly when the columns are orthonormal, so the inverse is just the transpose. Rotations and reflections are orthogonal and keep lengths and angles. A common mistake is thinking orthogonal columns are enough; they must also have length 1.
assumptions: Q square with orthonormal columns
det Q = ±1: +1 a rotation, −1 a reflection
related: a symmetric A is diagonalized by an orthogonal Q

example.problem: Check that Q = [0.6 −0.8; 0.8 0.6] is orthogonal, and write its inverse.

a · (b × c) = det[a; b; c].title: Scalar triple product
a · (b × c) = det[a; b; c].about: The signed volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c; zero means coplanar. b × c is the base's area times its normal; dotting with a takes the height. A common mistake is forgetting the absolute value for a volume.
assumptions: 3-D vectors
Signed: swapping two vectors flips the sign; its absolute value is the volume
related: det A = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg)

example.problem: Find the volume of the box on (1, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) and (0, 0, 3).

u = a/|a|.title: Unit vector
u = a/|a|.about: Dividing a vector by its length keeps its direction and makes its length 1. Use it to give a direction to a force or to project onto an axis. A common mistake is dividing by the sum of the components instead of the length.
related: projection uses the direction of b

example.problem: Find the unit vector along (1, 2, 2).

λ = T/2 ± √(T^{2}/4 − D).title: Eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix
λ = T/2 ± √(T^{2}/4 − D).about: Roots of λ² − Tλ + D = 0 with T the trace and D the determinant.
assumptions: A is 2 × 2
T^{2}/4 < D gives a complex pair: an oscillating mode

example.problem: Eigenvalues of [2 1; 1 2].

A = P D P^{−1}.title: Diagonalization
A = P D P^{−1}.about: With n independent eigenvectors, A is a diagonal matrix in that basis, so powers become easy: A^{k} = P D^{k} P^{−1}. It uncouples x′ = A x into one equation per mode. A common mistake is putting eigenvectors in P's rows; they are its columns.
assumptions: A has n independent eigenvectors (always so for n distinct eigenvalues, or a real symmetric A)
P's columns are in the same order as D's eigenvalues
related: the columns of P and entries of D

example.problem: [2 1; 1 2] has λ = 3, 1 with v = (1, 1), (1, −1). Diagonalize it, and check by multiplying back.

rank(A) + nullity(A) = n.title: Rank–nullity theorem
rank(A) + nullity(A) = n.about: Every column of A is either a pivot (independent) or free. Pivots count the rank; free columns each give a null-space direction.
assumptions: n is the number of columns, not rows
related: A x = b solvable ⇔ rank[A b] = rank(A)

example.problem: A 3 × 5 matrix has rank 3. How many free parameters does A x = 0 have?

A^{T} A x = A^{T} b.title: Least squares: the normal equations
A^{T} A x = A^{T} b.about: When A x = b has more equations than unknowns and no exact solution, the x that minimises |A x − b| solves this square system. It is how a line or curve is fitted to data.
assumptions: A has independent columns, so A^{T} A is invertible
For ill-conditioned A, QR is more accurate than forming A^{T} A
related: A x − b ⊥ columns of A

R_{i} ← R_{i} − (a_{ik}/a_{kk}) R_{k}.title: Gaussian elimination (row reduction)
R_{i} ← R_{i} − (a_{ik}/a_{kk}) R_{k}.about: The row operation that solves A x = b by hand: subtract a multiple of pivot row k from each row i below it to zero the entries under the pivot a_{kk}. Column by column on [A | b] it leaves an upper-triangular system, solved by back substitution from the last row up. It also finds rank, determinants and inverses (reduce [A | I]).
assumptions: the pivot a_{kk} is not zero; if it is, swap in a lower row with a nonzero entry (partial pivoting picks the largest, which also limits round-off)
apply each operation to the whole row, right-hand side b included
a row of zeros with a nonzero right side means no solution; a row of all zeros means a free variable (infinitely many)
vars: row i of the augmented matrix [A | b], the row being cleared
the pivot: the diagonal entry of column k
the entry in row i under the pivot, to be zeroed
related: the multipliers m_{ik} fill L, the reduced rows are U
the same answer by the inverse
rank: the pivots left after elimination

example.problem: Solve 2x + y = 5 and 4x + 3y = 13 by elimination.

f(x) = p(x)/q(x).title: Rational function and its asymptotes
f(x) = p(x)/q(x).about: A rational function is one polynomial over another. Its graph has a vertical asymptote where the denominator is zero (and the numerator isn't), and its end behaviour, the horizontal or slant asymptote, comes from the leading terms. Reach for it to sketch a graph or find a domain.
assumptions: Cancel common factors first: a zero shared by p and q is a hole, not an asymptote
deg p < deg q: horizontal asymptote y = 0
deg p = deg q: horizontal asymptote y = (leading coefficient of p)/(leading coefficient of q)
deg p = deg q + 1: a slant asymptote, the quotient from long division; deg p > deg q + 1: none
vars: denominator polynomial, q ≠ 0 on the domain
related: vertex of a quadratic, for sketching

example.problem: Find the asymptotes of f(x) = (2x^{2} + 3)/(x^{2} − 4).
steps: Vertical: x^{2} − 4 = 0 at x = ±2, and the numerator isn't zero there
Degrees equal (2 and 2): horizontal asymptote y = 2/1 = 2

|x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b.title: Absolute value inequality
|x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b.about: |x − a| is the distance from x to a, so |x − a| < b holds for the points within b of a: one interval. The opposite, |x − a| > b, holds outside it: x < a − b or x > a + b, two pieces.
assumptions: b > 0; if b ≤ 0, |x − a| < b has no solution
≤ gives a closed interval; > or ≥ gives two rays, joined by 'or'
Isolate the absolute value first: 2|x − 1| + 3 < 9 becomes |x − 1| < 3

example.problem: Solve |x − 3| < 5, and |x − 3| > 5.

sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan.title: SOH CAH TOA: trig ratios in a right triangle
sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan.about: In a right triangle, the sine, cosine and tangent of an acute angle θ are ratios of the sides: opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. Use them to find a side from an angle, or an angle from two sides with the inverse functions.
assumptions: The triangle has a right angle; for any triangle use the laws of sines and cosines
Opposite and adjacent are relative to θ; the hypotenuse is always the side across from the right angle
θ = sin^{−1}(opp/hyp) etc. gives the angle; set the calculator to degrees or radians to match
vars: an acute angle of the triangle
side next to θ, not the hypotenuse

example.problem: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall at 60° to the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The height is opposite the 60° angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse
opp = hyp sin θ = 5 m × sin 60° = 5 × 0.8660

y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D.title: Graph of a sinusoid: amplitude, period, phase shift
y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D.about: Every sine or cosine graph is the basic one stretched and shifted. |A| is the amplitude (half the peak-to-peak height), 2π/B the period, C the horizontal (phase) shift and D the midline. Read these off to sketch the graph or write its equation.
assumptions: B > 0; factor B out first: sin(2x − π/2) = sin(2(x − π/4)), so the shift is π/4, not π/2
x in radians for period 2π/B; in degrees the period is 360°/B
A < 0 flips the graph about its midline; the range is D − |A| to D + |A|
The same reading works for cos
related: a cos(θ) + b sin(θ) = R cos(θ − φ)
a sum of sinusoids as one

example.problem: Give the amplitude, period, phase shift and range of y = 3 sin(2(x − π/4)) + 1.
steps: Phase shift π/4 to the right
example.answer: amplitude 3, period π ≈ 3.1416, shift π/4 right, range [−2, 4]

dQ/dt = c_{in} r_{in} − (Q/V) r_{out}.title: Mixing tank: rate in minus rate out
dQ/dt = c_{in} r_{in} − (Q/V) r_{out}.about: The amount of dissolved stuff Q in a well-stirred tank changes at the rate it flows in (inflow concentration times inflow rate) minus the rate it flows out (the tank's concentration Q/V times the outflow rate). It is a first-order linear equation; with equal flows it is also separable.
assumptions: The tank is perfectly mixed: the outflow has the tank's concentration Q/V
If r_{in} ≠ r_{out}, the volume changes: V = V_{0} + (r_{in} − r_{out}) t, and the equation is linear, not separable
Equal flows: Q → c_{in} V with time constant V/r
vars: amount of solute in the tank

example.problem: A 100 L tank of pure water takes in brine at 0.2 kg/L and 5 L/min, and drains at 5 L/min. How much salt is in it after 20 min?
steps: Final value 20 kg, time constant 20 min: Q = 20(1 − e^{−t/20})

y_{2} = y_{1} ∫ e^{−∫ p dt}/y_{1}^{2} dt.title: Reduction of order: a second solution from one
y_{2} = y_{1} ∫ e^{−∫ p dt}/y_{1}^{2} dt.about: When you know one solution y₁ of a second-order linear homogeneous equation, this gives a second, independent one. It is how the repeated-root solution t e^{rt} arises, and it works for variable coefficients too.
assumptions: Put the equation in standard form y′′ + p y′ + q y = 0 first (divide by the y′′ coefficient)
y₁ must not be zero on the interval
Any constant from the integrals can be dropped: it only adds a multiple of y₁
vars: coefficient of y′ in standard form
related: a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0

example.problem: y′′ − 4y′ + 4y = 0 has the solution y₁ = e^{2t}. Find a second.
steps: y₁^{2} = e^{4t}, so the integrand is 1 and its integral is t

ℒ{y′} = s Y − y(0).title: Laplace transform of a derivative
ℒ{y′} = s Y − y(0).about: Taking the Laplace transform turns a derivative into multiplication by s, with the initial value folded in. So a linear ODE with constant coefficients becomes algebra in Y(s): solve for Y, then invert with the table and partial fractions.
assumptions: y and y′ are piecewise continuous and of exponential order
y(0) is the value just before t = 0 (y(0⁻)) when there is a jump
vars: Y(s) = ℒ{y(t)}, the transform of the unknown
related: the solution the inverse transform gives

example.problem: Solve y′ + 3y = 0, y(0) = 2, and find y(0.5).

ℒ{y′′} = s^{2} Y − s y(0) − y′(0).title: Laplace transform of a second derivative
ℒ{y′′} = s^{2} Y − s y(0) − y′(0).about: The second derivative transforms to s² times Y less the two initial conditions. This is how a second-order initial value problem, a spring-mass or RLC circuit, becomes one algebraic equation for Y(s).
assumptions: Constant coefficients; y, y′ and y′′ of exponential order
Both initial values y(0) and y′(0) enter, so no constants are left to fit at the end
related: its denominator is the characteristic polynomial

example.problem: Solve y′′ + 4y = 0, y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0, and find y(1).

ℒ{u(t − a) f(t − a)} = e^{−as} F(s).title: Step forcing: the second shifting theorem
ℒ{u(t − a) f(t − a)} = e^{−as} F(s).about: A forcing switched on at t = a is written with the unit step u(t − a). Its transform is the unshifted transform times e^{−as}; going back, a factor e^{−as} in Y(s) means delay the inverse by a and switch it on at a.
assumptions: Write the forcing as a function of (t − a) first: u(t − 1) t = u(t − 1)((t − 1) + 1)

example.problem: Solve y′ + y = u(t − 1), y(0) = 0, and find y(3).

ℒ{δ(t − a)} = e^{−as}.title: Impulse forcing: transform of the Dirac delta
ℒ{δ(t − a)} = e^{−as}.about: A sudden blow at t = a, a hammer strike or a charge dumped at once, is modelled by the delta δ(t − a), whose transform is just e^{−as}. The response to it is the impulse response, delayed to a.
assumptions: a ≥ 0; δ has unit area: ∫ δ(t − a) dt = 1
An impulse of size P is P δ(t − a)
It jumps y′ (for a second-order equation), not y
related: ℒ{u(t − a) f(t − a)} = e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: Solve y′′ + y = δ(t − π) from rest, and find y at t = 3π/2.

(A − λI) v = 0.title: Finding eigenvectors
(A − λI) v = 0.about: For each eigenvalue λ, row reduce A − λI and solve for its null space: every nonzero v there is an eigenvector. A repeated λ may give fewer independent vectors than its multiplicity (then A is not diagonalizable).
assumptions: λ a root of det(A − λI) = 0
v ≠ 0; any multiple is also an eigenvector

example.problem: A = [2 1; 1 2], λ = 3. Find a unit eigenvector.
steps: A − 3I = [−1 1; 1 −1]: the rows say v₁ = v₂

λ^{3} − tr(A) λ^{2} + (M_{11} + M_{22} +.title: Characteristic polynomial of a 3 × 3 matrix
λ^{3} − tr(A) λ^{2} + (M_{11} + M_{22} +.about: Expanding det(A − λI) for a 3 × 3 always gives this: the trace, the sum of the three principal 2 × 2 minors (delete row i and column i), and the determinant. Find one root by trying factors of det A, then divide down to a quadratic.
assumptions: A is 3 × 3
M_{ii}: determinant of A with row i and column i removed
related: det A = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg)

example.problem: A = [2 0 0; 0 3 4; 0 4 9]. Find the eigenvalues.
steps: λ = 1 is a root; the rest give λ = 2 and 11

λ_{i} = a_{ii}.title: Eigenvalues of a triangular matrix
λ_{i} = a_{ii}.about: For an upper or lower triangular (or diagonal) matrix, det(A − λI) is the product of (a_{ii} − λ), so the eigenvalues are read straight off the diagonal. Row reduction changes eigenvalues, so this only applies to A itself.
assumptions: A triangular or diagonal

example.problem: A = [3 5 1; 0 −2 4; 0 0 7]. Eigenvalues and det A?

A^{k} = P D^{k} P^{−1}.title: Matrix powers by diagonalization
A^{k} = P D^{k} P^{−1}.about: If A = PDP^{−1}, the inner P^{−1}P pairs cancel, so A^{k} needs only the k-th powers of the eigenvalues. Used for Markov chains, recurrences (Fibonacci) and discrete systems x_{k+1} = Ax_{k}.
assumptions: A diagonalizable: n independent eigenvectors

e^{At} = P e^{Dt} P^{−1}.title: Matrix exponential by diagonalization
e^{At} = P e^{Dt} P^{−1}.about: The system x′ = Ax has solution x(t) = e^{At}x(0). With A = PDP^{−1}, e^{At} = P diag(e^{λ_{i}t}) P^{−1}, so each mode decays or grows at its eigenvalue.
assumptions: A diagonalizable; otherwise use the Jordan form or the Laplace transform (sI − A)^{−1}
related: the same solution, mode by mode

A = U Σ V^{T}.title: Singular value decomposition (SVD)
A = U Σ V^{T}.about: Any m × n matrix factors as an orthogonal U, a diagonal Σ of singular values σ_{1} ≥ σ_{2} ≥ … ≥ 0, and an orthogonal V^{T}. The σ_{i} are √(eigenvalues of A^{T}A); V holds those eigenvectors. Used for rank, the 2-norm (σ_{1}), the condition number σ_{1}/σ_{n} and low-rank approximation.
assumptions: Exists for every real matrix
Rank = number of nonzero σ_{i}

example.problem: Find the singular values of A = [3 0; 4 5].

A^{−1} = C^{T}/det(A).title: Inverse by the adjugate (cofactors)
A^{−1} = C^{T}/det(A).about: Each entry of the inverse is a cofactor over the determinant, transposed: (A^{−1})_{ij} = C_{ji}/det A, with C_{ij} = (−1)^{i+j} M_{ij}. Handy for one entry of a 3 × 3 inverse; row reduction of [A | I] is faster for the whole thing.
assumptions: det A ≠ 0
Mind the transpose: row i of the inverse uses column i of cofactors
vars: minor: det with row i, column j removed

rank(A) = rank([A | b]).title: When A x = b has a solution
rank(A) = rank([A | b]).about: Row reduce the augmented matrix [A | b]. If b adds a pivot (a row 0 … 0 | c with c ≠ 0) the system is inconsistent. Otherwise it is solvable: one solution if rank = n (no free variables), infinitely many if rank < n.
assumptions: A is m × n
related: the best answer when there is none

example.problem: x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 5. How many solutions?
steps: rank A = 1, but [A | b] reduces to a row 0 0 | 1: rank 2

P = A(A^{T} A)^{−1} A^{T}.title: Projection onto the column space
P = A(A^{T} A)^{−1} A^{T}.about: P b is the point in the column space of A closest to b, p = A x̂ from least squares; b − p is orthogonal to every column. P is symmetric and P^{2} = P. For one column a it is aa^{T}/(a^{T}a).
assumptions: A has independent columns
vars: matrix whose columns span the subspace

example.problem: Project b = (1, 2, 2) onto the line through a = (1, 1, 1).

u_{k} = v_{k} − Σ_{j<k} ((v_{k} · u_{j}).title: Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization
u_{k} = v_{k} − Σ_{j<k} ((v_{k} · u_{j}).about: Turn independent vectors v_{1}, v_{2}, … into an orthogonal set: from each v_{k} subtract its projections onto the u's already found, then divide each u by its length for an orthonormal basis. It builds the Q of A = QR.
assumptions: v's linearly independent; a zero u means v_{k} was dependent

example.problem: Orthogonalize v₁ = (1, 1, 0), v₂ = (1, 0, 1). How long is u₂?
steps: u₁ = v₁; v₂ · u₁ = 1, u₁ · u₁ = 2

A = Q R.title: QR factorization
A = Q R.about: A with independent columns factors into Q (orthonormal columns, from Gram–Schmidt) and upper triangular R = Q^{T}A. Least squares then becomes R x = Q^{T}b, solved by back substitution, which is better conditioned than the normal equations.
assumptions: A m × n with independent columns

example.problem: A has columns (1, 1, 0) and (1, 0, 1). Find r₁₁.
